newsitem.title: USA: Democratic senator tips balance against amendment.
newsitem.headline: Democratic senator tips balance against amendment.

text.p: Democratic Sen. Robert Torricelli on Wednesday dealt a knockout punch to chances for approval of a constitutional amendment to balance the budget, refusing to cast the deciding vote for passage.

"I have struggled with this decision more than any I have ever made in my life," Torricelli, a freshman senator from New Jersey said at a news conference that ended days of speculation on whether Republicans could find the votes to pass the amendment.
The White House welcomed his decision, spokesman Mike McCurry said. "The president has opposed the amendment so he's glad in his conscience that Sen. Torricelli came to this judgment," he said.
Over the past 10 days, attention focused on four undecided freshmen Democrats who declared their intentions one-by-one until only Torricelli was left to tip the balance.

Republicans said they had not given up hope of finding a last minute vote, but the chief sponsor, Sen. Orrin Hatch, said he expected the result in next Tuesday's vote would be a 66-34 defeat. An amendment to the U.S. Constitution requires a two-thirds majority to pass.

Torricelli's decision spilled over into the House of Representatives where House leaders had hoped a Senate victory would give a boost to the amendment which was bogged down in committee over Republican concerns it could force Social Security cuts.
House Majority Leader Dick Armey told a small group of reporters he was still committed to passage. "I would still expect a vote before the year is over," he said.

But the situation would have to calm down before a decision is made. "It is sort of like a blast of lightning. The herd gets jumpy and you have to ride around once until they settle down," Armey, a Texas Republican, said.

Torricelli's main objections concerned the inflexibility of the balanced budget amendment in response to downturns in the economy, preparations for war and the need for long-term investments in highways, schools and bridges. His own proposal to add this flexibility failed 37-63 on Wednesday. Other Democratic alternatives were also defeated.

Torricelli, who won after one of the year's most negative Senate campaigns, said his decision was not inconsistent with his campaign pledge to support a balanced budget amendment or his past votes in the House for proposed budget amendments.

He said he did not commit to vote only for the Republican version and would continue to support Democratic alternatives. He did not believe the proposed Republican plan met the high test needed for a change to the constitution.
"All doubts concerning amendments to the Constitution of the United States must be settled in favour of leaving the genius of the Founding Fathers undisturbed," he said.
"Amending the Constitution is unlike any other action taken by the Congress," he said. "These are words that will govern contingencies that we cannot imagine, circumstances that we cannot foresee."
The amendment is opposed by President Clinton, whose main argument has been a warning to the public of potential cuts in Social Security benefits if it is passed.
Senate Republicans said the Social Security issue was political cover raised by the White House and Democrats for those who do not want to vote for the amendment.
Federal Reserve Board chairman Alan Greenspan has repeatedly told lawmakers the balanced budget amendment is not a good idea, but he continues to urge the budget be balanced.

Work on that front would continue unaffected by the balanced budget amendment vote. Budget committees were to begin action on the fiscal 1998 budget next month and Armey told reporters Republicans would discuss specific funding levels with the administration.

The balanced budget amendment has been in the works for 21 years but came closest to passage in 1995, when Republian Sen. Mark Hatfield of Oregon cast the deciding vote against it. It passed the House that year.

The amendment would require a balanced federal budget by 2002 or within two years of its enactment, but does not specify how Congress should do this, and would permit deficits and borrowing if approved by three-fifths of Congress. If it were approved it would have to be ratified by 38 of 50 states.
